technique_name: WebShell
description: An attacker may exploit a web shell backdoor on a web server to establish persistent access to the system. A web shell is a web script placed on a publicly accessible web server, which allows the attacker to use the web server as a network gateway. A web shell can provide a set of functions or command-line interfaces to be executed on the system hosting the web server.
potential_defenses: Use the company's WSF framework for protection.
detection_opportunities: Static feature detection refers to the process of identifying multiple dimensions of features within script files. These features include keywords, high-risk functions, file modification times, file permissions, file owners, and associations with other files. Typically, a malicious string feature database is first established. For example, the database may include entries such as "WScript.Shell, Shell.Application, Eval(), Execute(), Set Server, Run(), Exec(), ShellExecute()". At the same time, the modification time of the web file, file permissions, and file owner are all confirmed. Under normal circumstances, web files will not contain the above-mentioned features or will have abnormal features. By comparing and searching against the feature database, high-risk script files can be identified.
code_examples_patterns: Upload malicious script (e.g., .php, .jsp, .aspx) to web root directory
Access web shell via HTTP to execute arbitrary commands on the server

technique_name: Modify the Authentication Module > Modifying the PAM component to implant a backdoor
description: Attackers can modify the components of PAM modules, such as pam_unix.so, to implant backdoors. This allows attackers to access the system through specific accounts.
potential_defenses: Use multi-factor authentication
detection_opportunities: Monitor file modifications related to the PAM mechanism.
code_examples_patterns: Modify PAM configuration files (e.g., /etc/pam.d/) to inject backdoor authentication logic
Replace or patch pam_unix.so with a backdoored version

technique_name: Modify System Image > Modify the system image file to implant a hardcoded password
description: Attackers implant hardcoded backdoors into the system image through patching, thereby maintaining access to network devices.
code_examples_patterns: Patch system image file to embed hardcoded backdoor credentials

technique_name: bootkit
description: Bootkit implants a backdoor by modifying the boot partition. It resides at a deeper level of the operating system and is often difficult to detect.
potential_defenses: Enabling secure boot verifies the integrity of the boot program.
code_examples_patterns: Modify boot partition (MBR/VBR) to load malicious code before OS

technique_name: Abuse of Traffic Signaling > Using Flow Signaling to Control Communication Ports
description: Attackers exploit traffic signaling to send packets containing special characters, thereby controlling the execution of malicious code on a remote server. This malicious code can be used to open or close specific ports, or to execute special commands, such as adding, deleting, or altering malicious functionalities.
code_examples_patterns: Craft packets with special signaling characters to trigger remote code execution

technique_name: Create a Scheduled Task > Create a Crontab Scheduled Task
description:
crontab is a command in the Linux system used to set up instructions that are executed periodically. If an attacker has the permission to modify crontab, they can add new crontab entries to execute attack scripts at scheduled times, thereby achieving persistent attacks.
The attack steps are as follows:
1. Enter the command `crontab -e` in the command line.
2. If the user has the necessary permissions, they will enter the editor mode and add a new line at the end of the file: `"* * * * * echo "test_cron" > /tmp/test_cron"`. (The above `echo` command is used for testing and can be replaced with a real malicious script.)
3. One minute later, check whether the above command has been successfully executed. (If the `echo` command is used, you can check with `ls -l /tmp/test_cron`.)
4. If the command is successfully executed, it indicates that the current user has the permission to modify crontab. According to the principle of least privilege, if it cannot be guaranteed that the current user requires this permission, then the permission should be denied.
5. Finally, use the command `crontab -e` again to clear the test scheduled task and restore the environment.
potential_defenses: Restrict user accounts' permission to modify the crontab.
detection_opportunities: Check whether there are any abnormal crontab entries. You can use the command `crontab -l` or inspect the directory `/var/spool/cron/crontabs`.
code_examples_patterns: Add malicious entry via crontab -e to execute payload at scheduled intervals
Inspect /var/spool/cron/crontabs for unauthorized entries

technique_name: Create a Startup Task > Creating a Global Autostart Task
description:
If an attacker has the permission to modify directories or files (such as rc.local, profile, and system) in /etc, the attacker can configure automatically executed commands or services to implement persistent attacks.
Take /etc/profile as an example. The attack procedure is as follows:
1. Run the ls command to check the permission on the /etc/profile file and the directory to which the file belongs. Check whether the current user has the permission to modify or replace the file. (If the file does not exist, check whether the user has the permission to create the file.)
2. If you have the modify/replace/create permission, add a command to the file, for example, echo "test_profile" > /tmp/test_profile. (The preceding echo command is used for testing and can be replaced with a real malicious script.)
3. Log in to the shell again. (The profile is loaded during login. Therefore, the test can be performed after login again. Some commands, such as rc.local, are loaded during system startup and need to be restarted.)
4. Check whether the added command (for example, ls -l /tmp/test_profile) is successfully executed. If the command is successfully executed, the current user has the permission to create global auto-start tasks. If there is no application scenario, this permission should be restricted.
5. Delete the added commands and restore the environment.
potential_defenses: Restrict user accounts from modifying permissions configured under /etc.
detection_opportunities: Check whether there are any abnormal entries in the relevant files. You can examine the contents of files such as /etc/rc*, /etc/profile, and /etc/services.
code_examples_patterns: Add malicious command to /etc/rc.local, /etc/profile, or /etc/services

technique_name: Create a Startup Task > Create a User Startup Task
description:
If an attacker can modify the configuration file (such as .profile and .bashrc) in the working directory of the current user, the attacker can configure the automatically executed command to implement persistent attacks against the current user permission.
Take ~/.profile as an example. The attack procedure is as follows:
1. Run the ls command to check the permission on the ~/.profile file and the directory to which the file belongs. Check whether the current user has the permission to modify or replace the file. (If the file does not exist, check whether the user has the permission to create the file.)
2. If you have the modify/replace/create permission, add a command to the file, for example, echo "test_profile" > /tmp/test_profile. (The preceding echo command is used for testing and can be replaced with a real malicious script.)
3. Log in to the shell again.
4. Check whether the added command (for example, ls -l /tmp/test_profile) is successfully executed. If the command is successfully executed, the current user has the permission to create a user auto-start task. If there is no application scenario, this permission should be restricted.
5. Delete the added commands and restore the environment.
potential_defenses: Restrict user accounts to modify related configuration files.
detection_opportunities: Check whether there are any abnormal entries in the relevant files. You can check the contents of files such as ~/.profile and ~/.bashrc.
code_examples_patterns: Add malicious command to ~/.profile or ~/.bashrc for user-level persistence

technique_name: Tampering with Binary Files > Tampering with Software Binary Files
description:
Attackers can modify software binary files on the target host to establish persistent access to the system, such as the SSH server and FTP server.
Take the SSH server as an example. The attack procedure is as follows: (The SSH service will be disabled during the test, and the SSH login will fail. You need to have the permission to log in to the server. Otherwise, you are not advised to test the SSH server. You can test other services, such as the FTP server.)
1. Run the ls command to check the permission on the /usr/sbin/sshd file and the directory to which the file belongs. Check whether the current user has the permission to modify or replace the file.
2. If you have the modify/replace permission, back up the sshd file (for example, cp sshd sshd sshd.bk), run the systemctl stop ssh command to stop the ssh service, and disconnect all SSH connections.
3. Modify the /usr/sbin/sshd file, for example, using echo -n "test" >> /usr/sbin/sshd or replacing it with an sshd file with a backdoor.
4. Run the xxd command to confirm that the sshd is modified, and then run the systemctl start ssh command to start the ssh service.
5. Use the modified SSH. If the SSH can be used properly, (If the backdoor sshd is used, the backdoor function can be used.), it indicates that the SSH server is modified and the backdoor is inserted into the attack mode. According to the principle of least permission, if the current user does not need the permission, disable the permission.
6. Use sshd.bk to replace sshd with sshd and restore the environment.
potential_defenses: Ensure that all program binaries are correctly signed.
code_examples_patterns: Replace or modify system binary (e.g., /usr/sbin/sshd) with backdoored version

technique_name: Using the Kubernetes Service to Attack > K8s cronjob Persistence
description: A Cronjob is used to create time-based scheduling tasks. After obtaining the controller create permission, an attacker can create a Cronjob to achieve persistence.
potential_defenses: Restrict the execution permissions of kubectl and separate them from the users running the applications.
detection_opportunities: Run the kubectl get cronjobs command to check whether abnormal cronjobs exist.
code_examples_patterns: Create malicious CronJob via kubectl create cronjob to maintain persistence

technique_name: Using the Kubernetes Service to Attack > Maintaining Backdoor Containers Through the K8s Controller
description: Attackers, through the controller, can not only achieve execution but also further configure the controller to set up and maintain backdoor containers on any Node. These containers can be configured as privileged containers and can further implant binaries into each Node by mounting the host machine's file space. This process completes the persistence at the Node layer, and subsequent operations will not trigger the audit policy at the K8s layer.
potential_defenses: Restrict the execution permissions of kubectl and separate them from the users running the applications.
detection_opportunities: Check whether there are any additional abnormal pods on the node.
code_examples_patterns: Deploy backdoor container via K8s Controller and mount host filesystem

technique_name: Exploiting Private Image Repositories for Attacks > Planting backdoors in images within a private image repository
description: If a private image repository is compromised by an attacker, the attacker can pull images to obtain information and update the images in the repository to malicious ones.
potential_defenses: Image release requires authentication and anonymous release is restricted.
detection_opportunities: Check the release history on the image repository.
code_examples_patterns: Push backdoored container image to private registry for supply chain persistence

technique_name: Container Escape Attack > Writing files to the host machine by mounting a directory
description: If the container incorrectly mounts key directories of the host machine, such as /etc and /root, an attacker can modify sensitive files on the host machine through the container. This allows the attacker to perform operations on the host machine and achieve persistence.
potential_defenses: Strictly inspect the mounted directories. It is strictly prohibited to mount sensitive system directories of the host machine.
code_examples_patterns: Write malicious files to host via mounted sensitive directory (e.g., /etc, /root)

technique_name: Exploiting Processes within a Container for Privilege Escalation
description:
Principle: If a program in a container invokes a low-privilege user process, attackers can tamper with the low-privilege user process to implement privilege escalation.
1. Use docker exec -it -u root dockerid bash to enter the inside of the container.
2. Run the ps -ef command to check whether the process in the container is run by the root user. If yes, check whether the start script is run by the ossadm user.
3. After the preceding requirements are met, modify the startup script as user ossadm, add useradd=test, and wait for user root to run the script.
4. Check whether the test user is added and privilege escalation is complete.
potential_defenses: Ensure that the container runs as a non-privileged user and does not have the permissions to perform privilege escalation operations.
code_examples_patterns: Tamper with low-privilege process/script inside container to escalate to root

technique_name: Exploiting Executable Scripts Inside Containers for Privilege Escalation
description:
Principle: If a program in a container invokes a low-privilege user script, attackers can tamper with the low-privilege process to escalate the privilege.
1. Use docker exec -it -u root dockerid bash to enter the inside of the container.
2. Run the find command to search for all scripts in the container. Check the user guide or command reference to check whether the script is executed by the root user.
3. If the script exists, modify the script as user ossadm and add the useradd=test command. Wait until the administrator executes the script according to the documentation requirements.
4. Check whether the test user is added and privilege escalation is complete.
potential_defenses: Ensure that executable scripts within the container run as a non-privileged user and do not have the permission to perform privilege escalation operations.
code_examples_patterns: Tamper with low-privilege process/script inside container to escalate to root

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > copy_from_user overflow
description: By exploiting the overflow of copy_from_user, one can overwrite kernel data structures or control the execution flow of the kernel.
potential_defenses: Before calling copy_from_user, a strict validation of the copy length is performed.
code_examples_patterns: Exploit copy_from_user overflow to overwrite kernel data structures

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > Copy_to_user Information Disclosure
description: By exploiting the overflow of copy_to_user, one can obtain kernel address/content information from memory.
potential_defenses: Before calling copy_to_user, a strict validation of the copy length is performed.
code_examples_patterns: Exploit copy_to_user overflow to leak kernel memory content

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > Any address in the kernel is writable.
description: When data is copied from user mode to kernel mode, kernel-mode overflow, array out-of-bounds, and the use of functions such as __put_user, __copy_to_user, writel function group, and memcpy, can be used to write to any address in the kernel.
potential_defenses:
Avoid using functions such as __put_user, __copy_from_user, and memcpy to directly copy user-mode data.
2. When using functions like writel, ensure that the addr parameter has been validated for legitimacy.
3. Before copying data, verify the length of the data.
4. When using arrays, pay attention to whether the array index will go out of bounds.
code_examples_patterns: Exploit unchecked user-to-kernel copy to write arbitrary kernel memory

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > Arbitrary kernel address readable
description: When data is copied from kernel mode to user mode, the content of any kernel address can be read, or the addresses of important kernel data structures can be leaked, through the use of kernel-mode overflows, array out-of-bounds, the readl function family, memcpy, and other functions.
potential_defenses:
When using functions such as readl, ensure that the addr parameter has been validated for legitimacy.
2. Before copying data, verify the length of the data.
3. When using arrays, pay attention to whether the array index will go out of bounds.
code_examples_patterns: Exploit unchecked kernel-to-user copy to read arbitrary kernel memory

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > Incorrect use of kernel lock mechanism
description: Due to logical errors in the lock's request and release processes, the kernel experiences a denial of service.
potential_defenses: Avoid situations where locking and unlocking are mismatched.
code_examples_patterns: Exploit mismatched lock/unlock to cause kernel denial of service

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > Kernel Mode Conditional Race
description: Insufficient protection of shared resources creates a time window where, in the event that multiple threads simultaneously use shared resources, it is possible to bypass validation, obtain resources, or execute code by exploiting thread contention/scheduling techniques.
potential_defenses:
Lock and protect shared resources in multi-threaded environments.
2. Avoid using shared resources in a way that leaves a window period between the validation and usage of the shared resource.
code_examples_patterns: Exploit TOCTOU race in shared resource access for privilege escalation

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > Signed Number Overflow
description: During the process of numerical computation, if a certain variable is a controllable variable, it can lead to signed integer overflow. Furthermore, if this variable is used as an index for an array at this point, it may cause stack overflow, privilege escalation,
potential_defenses: Before performing arithmetic operations on signed numbers, it is necessary to evaluate the upper and lower boundaries of the signed numbers, as well as the sign bit.
code_examples_patterns: Trigger signed integer overflow to cause out-of-bounds kernel access

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > Unsigned Number Overflow
description: During the process of numerical computation, if a certain variable is a controllable variable, it can cause unsigned integer overflow. Furthermore, if this variable is an index of an array at this time, it may cause stack overflow, privilege escalation,
potential_defenses: Before performing unsigned arithmetic operations, validate the upper and lower boundaries of the unsigned numbers.
code_examples_patterns: Trigger signed integer overflow to cause out-of-bounds kernel access

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > UAF Attack
description: Resources in the kernel, after calling functions such as kfree() or sk_put(), continue to be used. This can lead to a "use after free" issue.
potential_defenses:
Set the pointer to null after releasing it.
2. Do not reuse the pointer after it has been released.
code_examples_patterns: Exploit kernel UAF by reusing freed memory for arbitrary code execution

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > Set_fs does not restore the address limit.
description: Some modules in the kernel need to read and write user-space files. To achieve this, they call set_fs(KERNEL_DS) to temporarily change the addr_limit. However, in some exception handling branches, the addr_limit is not restored, leading to the absence of a boundary between kernel and user-space memory.
potential_defenses: Restore addr_limit in all branches (normal or abnormal).
code_examples_patterns: Exploit set_fs failure to bypass kernel/user memory boundary

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > Stack Overflow
description: By constructing shellcode, the stack structure of the buffer is destroyed, thereby achieving the purpose of executing the shellcode.
potential_defenses: Before using a buffer, strictly validate the length of the buffer.
code_examples_patterns: Construct shellcode to overflow kernel stack and execute arbitrary code

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > Prohibiting the referencing of uninitialized memory
description: By using an uninitialized kernel stack variable, it is possible to exploit a vulnerability that allows arbitrary writes to kernel addresses, thereby enabling privilege escalation attacks.
potential_defenses: Initialize memory stack variables that are not initialized before using them.
code_examples_patterns: Exploit uninitialized kernel stack variable for arbitrary write

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > Lack of boundary check results in out-of-bounds access.
description: The developer's external driver interface did not validate the input data, leading to an array out-of-bounds condition. By accessing content constructed in a specific manner, the attacker was able to perform a privilege escalation attack.
potential_defenses: For data passed through external interfaces, the program should validate the legitimacy of the external data.
code_examples_patterns: Exploit missing boundary check in driver interface for privilege escalation

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > null pointer dereference
description: The program attempts to dereference a pointer that should have been valid but is instead NULL. This results in a program crash, exit, or privilege escalation operation.
potential_defenses:
Enable the mmap_min_addr feature, which prevents user space from mapping at low addresses.
2. When dereferencing a pointer, ensure that the value is not NULL.
code_examples_patterns: Exploit null pointer dereference to crash kernel or escalate privileges

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > Kernel Division by Zero Exception
description: The system generates an exception for division by zero operations, leading to a denial of service.
potential_defenses: To address data other than zero, it is necessary to avoid such data and adjust it to an appropriate value.
code_examples_patterns: Trigger division by zero in kernel to cause denial of service

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > Kernel Pointer Information Leakage
description: %p prints pointer information and leaks the kernel address.
potential_defenses: All occurrences of %p in kernel code printing must be replaced with %pK.
code_examples_patterns: Exploit %p format string in kernel print to leak kernel addresses

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > Address Randomization Bypass
description: By rewriting addr_limit, arbitrary address write operations in the kernel can be achieved. After reading a specific offset, the thread_info information can be obtained.
potential_defenses: Restore addr_limit in all branches (normal or abnormal).
code_examples_patterns: Rewrite addr_limit to bypass address randomization and read kernel data

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > String Formatting Attack
description: String Formatting Attack
potential_defenses: When using a formatted string, the number of variables in the string must be equal to the number of input/output variables in the function.
code_examples_patterns: Exploit format string vulnerability in kernel for arbitrary read/write

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > Kernel Type Obfuscation Attack
description: Using one data type as another can lead to illegal access, program crashes, or the execution of malicious code.
potential_defenses: Examine the type of an object before using it.
code_examples_patterns: Exploit kernel type confusion to trigger illegal memory access

technique_name: Kernel Component Code Attack > Kernel Logic Error
description: There are logical errors in the system kernel or drivers, such as a condition judgment that is always true, or the presence of dead code.
potential_defenses: Review the code to identify and resolve logical issues.
code_examples_patterns: Exploit always-true condition or dead code in kernel for DoS or escalation

technique_name: Kernel Fuzzing Attack > Syzkaller Kernel Fuzz Attack
description: Using the Syzkaller tool for Fuzzing
potential_defenses: Not involved
code_examples_patterns: Use syzkaller to fuzz kernel syscalls and discover vulnerabilities

technique_name: Kernel Bytecode Tampering > Kernel Rookit Technology Tampers bytecode
description: After obtaining the permission to execute code in kernel mode, the attacker dynamically tampers with the kernel bytecode to carry out covert and persistent attacks.
code_examples_patterns: Dynamically patch kernel bytecode in kernel mode for covert persistence
